title: Matter near absolute zero
question: What happens to a gas of bosons close to absolute zero?
hook: Cool the right atoms enough and a large share of them pile into one quantum state.
idea: Cooled very close to absolute zero, a dilute gas of bosons can fall into the lowest quantum state together, forming a Bose–Einstein condensate.

beats.prompt: A dilute cloud of bosonic atoms is cooled to very close to absolute zero. Where do many of them end up?

choices.label: Together in the lowest quantum state
Spread evenly across the higher energy levels
choices.feedback: Cooling pushes bosons downward: a large fraction occupy the lowest state.

choices.label: Each in its own separate state
choices.feedback: Bosons are allowed to share a state, so they are not forced apart like fermions.

beats.explain: Einstein proposed that cooling bosonic atoms to a very low temperature would make them condense into the lowest accessible quantum state.

items: London proposes it as a mechanism for superfluidity (1938)
Cornell and Wieman make the first gaseous condensate (1995)
beats.explain: The prediction came first, then London's proposal, then the 1995 rubidium condensate, and last the 1998 hydrogen one.

beats.prompt: Match each person to their role.
pairs: Made a condensate from rubidium atoms
Made a condensate from sodium atoms
Wrote the quantum statistics paper Einstein built on
Proposed it as a mechanism for superfluidity
beats.explain: Bose's paper led to Einstein's prediction, London linked it to superfluidity, and Cornell, Wieman and Ketterle made the first gaseous condensates.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Bosons are allowed to share a quantum state.
Cooling bosons close to absolute zero lets a large fraction occupy the lowest state.
Helium-3 atoms are bosons, so helium-3 must condense the same way.
So helium-3 should become superfluid at the same temperature as helium-4.
beats.explain: A helium-3 atom is a fermion, which forms bosonic pairs only at a much lower temperature.
